builder_plan.scenario: Your coding assistant makes changes that still need substantial repair before merging.
builder_plan.change: Try the technique on held-out issues from a repository with reliable tests.
builder_plan.baseline: The same coding agent, repository snapshot, tools, and token budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct patches, regression failures, human repair time, and total cost per accepted change.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: DARE: Difficulty Analysis for Repair Enhancement
summary: The method replaces uniform agent support and difficulty assessment based on solve rates with a framework that uses 151 static features to predict task failure rates and select task-specific support. It costs the engineering complexity of extracting feature groups and the computational expense of initially establishing ground-truth failure rates across multiple agents. It can fail if the moderate correlation (rho = .476-.621) misidentifies task difficulty, leading to mismatched support and suboptimal repair outcomes.
rationale: It offers a practical method to improve automated program repair success on constrained infrastructure by matching support strategies to predicted task difficulty, though the moderate predictive accuracy requires validation on specific workloads.

claims.statement: The method replaces uniform agent support and difficulty assessment based on solve rates with a framework that uses 151 static features to predict task failure rates and select task-specific support. It costs the engineering complexity of extracting feature groups and the computational expense of initially establishing ground-truth failure rates across multiple agents. It can fail if the moderate correlation (rho = .476-.621) misidentifies task difficulty, leading to mismatched support and suboptimal repair outcomes.

The difficulty model's aligned predictions achieve Spearman's rho = .476-.621 on held-out partitions, and coding-agent experiments show improved repair success when support is matched to each task's salient Feature Group.
